b.x: This is a story for reflection. It does not teach looting, gangs, breaking in, or a weapon. It is not a forecast. While the phone still lives, 192, 190, and 193 are on the red page. This page does not dial.

Elias Rezende lived on the fourth floor with Lena and two small children. Across the hall, Davi lived with Nara and two others, the same age. Davi was the man who laughed. When Elias filled bottles, Davi said the world does not end on a Tuesday. When Elias spoke of a paper with a street name, Davi said that was movie fear. Elias did not argue. He had read the manual until the count closed: water, food the mouth already accepts, gas, one light, soap, the medicine of whoever already takes it, small cash, and a closed mouth. His mind was not a gift. It was the habit of seeing what was in front of him and not what he preferred. Lena knew the count. The children knew the flashlight was not a toy.

The power fell in the afternoon, and it did not return anywhere the radio could still reach. Dead traffic lights. A mute card. A stopped elevator. For a while the phone still searched for the tower. Then that ended too. Davi laughed in the hall. One hour, he said. Maybe the night. He opened the refrigerator for a warm beer and left the door open while he talked. Elias closed his. He filled whatever the tap still gave. He checked the spare cylinder. He turned on one light. He counted four people. Lena put the children on the small task of always: washed feet, a cup, a short story. Nobody in that house announced what was behind the door. On the street, the small market was still selling. The line took water and bread. Elias did not go down. The first day does not kill by hunger. It kills by hurry.

On the second day the beer was gone and Davi's meat smelled. The water on the high floor failed. Nara knocked on Elias's door with the child's cup. Elias gave the cup. He did not open the pantry. Davi, behind her, still found a way to call that exaggeration. On the fourth day the big market was a crowd. On the fifth, Davi went. He came back without water, with a swollen fist, and without the joke. He did not say what he saw. His children drank little. On the sixth day Elias looked from the dark window and saw three men at the market door who on the first day had been in the line, like everyone. On the sixth, they were not buying. They were staying. That was enough. He did not go down to confirm. Lena already knew the morning written on the paper. Their house ate the usual plate through the seventh day. They drank on a count. The children slept. The other house fought, in a voice that crossed the wall, about whose idea it had been to store nothing.

Elias's count was seven days well, not a year of tins. He did not pretend the pantry was infinite. On the eighth day, early, the four went down the stairs with the bag that looked like travel. Not in the dark before dawn. Not one alone. Lena carried the girl. Elias carried the boy when the step failed. On the paper there was a sister's house, with a tank filled on the first day, two neighborhoods on foot. Davi was in the hall. This time he did not laugh. He asked if the power was coming back. Elias said he did not know. He said the name of the street, once, low. He did not say what he was still carrying. Davi stayed. The street, that morning, still let pass a family that looked like it was moving house, not a family that looked rich in food. Elias saw the whole corner before he entered it. Where there was a cluster, he turned. Where there was a shout, he did not go to look. An eagle's eye, in him, was not height. It was not needing to get close in order to understand.

Whoever stayed saw the month without needing a newspaper. The garbage stayed. The smell stayed. The dirty hand made people sick before the film's hunger. The market, from the sixth day on, was no longer a shopping line. It was a door with a new owner. A movie gang was not born. A group was born that noticed the city without power answers whoever stands at the door. First they stopped what they called a mess. Then they charged to let people pass. Then they knocked where there was light in the window. That is what the story needs you to understand. It does not need you to learn how to be them. A candle near a curtain burned an apartment on the tenth day. The rumor ran faster than the water. They said the power would return on Friday. On Friday it did not. They said there was a truck in the other neighborhood. The truck was not the danger. The road to the rumor was.

Davi waited. Waiting was what remained of the man who had mocked the paper. The children asked for water in a voice that was no longer a tantrum. They drank what they found. The younger one got sick. Nara looked at the name of the street Elias had said, written by her own hand on a bread paper, and on the eighteenth day she went down with the two. Davi said it was the madness of someone who believes a manual. Nara said the children were not going to wait for the joke to come back. She crossed early, the way he had crossed, without looking as if she carried the little that remained. She arrived at Elias's sister's house at the end of the light. Lena opened. There was no speech. There was a cup, soap, and a corner to sleep. Elias did not ask where Davi was. The house did not become a public shelter. It became seven people counting the tank's water, not four. The count changed. The rule did not. Nobody lit the window.

On the twenty-second Davi arrived. Thinner. Without the ready sentence. He did not come in as a man who had been right. He came in as a man who had walked too far. Nara did not shout. His children were alive, weak, and washed. The sister's house was not plenty. The plate, at the end of the month, was smaller. The tank's water was counted. The gas was Elias's spare, used slowly. There was no hero in the window. There was a bedtime and one light, away from the cloth. On the thirtieth day a rumor ran that in another district a lamp had flickered. Elias did not go out to see. This time Davi did not either. They stayed. The world outside still had no proof. Inside there were eight people who still chose the next day. Davi looked at the hall that was not his and said, low, that he had laughed at the bottle. Elias said the bottle did not ask for an apology. It asked to have been filled before. Nara's girl slept in Lena's arms. That was the whole month, summed up in that small weight.

Reset Mundial is not the end of the world. It is a month in which the grid leaves and what you did before remains. Elias did not become king of the street. He did not face the group at the door. He did not save the building. He saw early, ate what the house already ate, gave a cup without opening the pantry, and left on the day the count ended, with the whole family, looking like ordinary people. The expanded mind, in him, was not a light in the dark. It was not living inside the film. Davi was not evil. He was the man who thought mocking was thinking. The mockery cost two children their thirst. What took them out of the building was not a speech. It was Nara, with a street name on a bread paper. If this story is good for anything, it is for this: fill the water before Tuesday. Teach the house. Do not light the window. Do not wait for the thirtieth day to believe the sixth. And when the count ends, leave early, together, with no audience.
